title: Nvidia Is the Worst-Performing "Magnificent Seven" Stock This Year. Is It a Buy Before 2027?
detail:
Nvidia Is the Worst-Performing "Magnificent Seven" Stock This Year. Is It a Buy Before 2027?
Daniel Foelber, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 5:50 PM EST 6 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) investors have been on a rather unenjoyable roller coaster in recent weeks. And every time the ride looks like it's nearing an end, there's another unexpected turn that unearths more questions than answers.

Founder and CEO for over 33 years, Jensen Huang, admitted on Nov. 8 to being unfaithful to his wife, then resigned on Nov. 12, only to be brought back as CEO less than two weeks later on Nov. 23.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That same day, President Trump was on a phone interview with CNBC and took credit for speaking with Nvidia's board and helping convince them to bring Huang back. Trump said, "I spoke to them. Let me just put it that way. And I convinced them. And I will tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago." Trump was referring to Nvidia's stock price and how it was easier to convince Nvidia to bring Huang back when the stock was cratering.

Nvidia has rallied substantially since Huang came back as CEO, but Huang and Nvidia still face an uphill climb of federal, state, and internal investigations linked to Nvidia misleading investors and potential national security violations regarding advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence (AI) chips leaking into China through backdoor channels.

The stock is still under $100 per share at the time of this writing and down 20% year to date -- making it the worst-performing "Magnificent Seven" stock in 2026. The Magnificent Seven consists of seven mega-cap tech-focused companies that include Nvidia, Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA).

Here's the simplest reason to buy Nvidia, and an argument for why it's best to keep the semiconductor stock on a watch list for now.

Image source: Getty Images.

Nvidia is dirt cheap

Heading into this year, some investors were concerned that Nvidia would be unable to maintain its breakneck revenue growth rate and high gross margins. But hyperscalers continued to ramp up AI capital expenditures. And Nvidia has broadened its customer base to other enterprises, AI start-ups, AI labs, and neoclouds.

As a result, Nvidia's earnings growth began outpacing its stock price growth, compressing its valuation. But then the unthinkable happened.

title: 2 Dividend Stocks to Buy in November and 1 to Leave on the Shelf
detail:
2 Dividend Stocks to Buy in November and 1 to Leave on the Shelf
Reuben Gregg Brewer, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 6:45 PM EST 5 min read
MO
MKC
PG
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Altria's (NYSE:MO) 5.9% yield is very attractive, but don't rush out and buy the stock. You may be better off with McCormick's (NYSE:MKC) 4.1%, or even Procter & Gamble's (NYSE:PG) 2.5%. Here's why two of these stocks could be buys in November, and one is likely best left on the shelf.

Altria's yield is a warning sign

Altria isn't at any risk of going bankrupt. And its dividend doesn't look particularly risky, either. For more aggressive dividend investors, it may be worth a closer look given its well-above-market 5.9% yield. However, you have to ask yourself why that yield is so high before you buy the stock.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

The answer is that Altria's combustible tobacco business, largely cigarettes, accounted for $5.4 billion of its $6.1 billion in revenues in the third quarter of 2026. That's 88% of the top line, which is a big problem when you consider that the number of cigarettes and cigars the company sold fell 2.9% in the quarter to 16.2 billion. In the third quarter of 2021, the company sold nearly 24.5 billion, indicating that this is a long-term trend. To be fair, Altria is working hard to diversify its business away from smokeable products, but given the uncertainty in the market today, thanks to geopolitical conflict, inflation, belt-tightening consumers, and AI volatility, why take on that kind of business risk?

Procter & Gamble is fairly priced and predictable

At the other end of the risk spectrum is Procter & Gamble, one of the world's largest consumer-staples makers. The company sells paper products, toiletries, and makeup, with its brands typically positioned at the high end of the market. While there is some trade-down risk in that market position, P&G has long focused on leading the consumer staples sector with innovation. The goal is to produce products that consumers are willing to pay more for because they get more from them.

Right now, P&G's 2.5% yield is well above the market's 1% and the consumer staples average of 2%. So you aren't skimping on yield to own this well-run company. That said, its price-to-sales and price-to-earnings ratios are roughly in line with their five-year averages, so you aren't getting a bargain price, either. However, given that P&G was able to increase its organic sales growth by a respectable 4% in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 despite increasingly cost-conscious consumers, conservative dividend investors should probably give it a closer look.

title: Prediction: These 3 Consumer Stocks Will Beat the S&P 500 Over the Next 10 Years
detail:
Prediction: These 3 Consumer Stocks Will Beat the S&P 500 Over the Next 10 Years
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 5:50 PM EST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Beating the S&P 500 sounds simple until you remember how good the index already is, since it has compounded at about 9.9% a year on a total return basis going back to 1928. So a stock that beats the index over 10 years needs more than a good quarter, it needs a business that can keep growing over the long term.

When I look for that kind of staying power in the consumer world, I aim for three things: a brand that people pay up for, a long expansion runway, and a management team that protects both. Here are three consumer stocks that I think long-term investors should consider for the decade ahead.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Ferrari: Fewer cars, more value

Ferrari (NYSE:RACE) deliberately builds fewer cars than people want, and that scarcity is the heart of its economic moat, which is a durable advantage that keeps rivals from stealing its customers.

CEO Benedetto Vigna said in the third-quarter release that deliveries "reflect our clients' ever-deepening desire to make each Ferrari uniquely their own." Those personal touches add profit to every car without adding volume.

Demand isn't the problem. Vigna said on the call, "We continue to experience a healthy demand across all geographies, with an order book that enters 2028."

The risks are a premium valuation, at roughly 36 times earnings, and the shift to electric models like the Luce, which has to win over buyers who love engines.

2. Hilton: Plenty of rooms left to fill

Hilton (NASDAQ:HLT) mostly doesn't own its hotels; it collects fees by managing and licensing its brands to owners through a franchise model, which is an arrangement where a business pays to use another company's brand and systems. That lets it grow without spending heavily on buildings.

CEO Chris Nassetta said in the third-quarter release, "We achieved our highest quarter ever for organic openings." He also said on the call, "Globally, Hilton is still less than 6% of supply providing a long runway for continued growth."

Travel is cyclical, though. CFO Kevin Jacobs said, "RevPAR in China declined 5.4% in the quarter," referring to revenue per available room, which is a key hotel measure of how well rooms are filled and priced. Middle East conflict is weighing on that region, too, and the stock trades near 49 times earnings.

Jensen Huang's return as CEO doesn't make Nvidia (NVDA) stock a Buy, despite the market's positive reaction. Shares of the leading semiconductor manufacturer jumped roughly 31.5% on November 23 after Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Huang with immediate effect. Yet the stock remains down roughly 31% over the past month following a steep sell-off.

Although Nvidia enjoys a long runway for growth, I believe investors should closely watch the regulatory scrutiny still surrounding the company. In the short term, Nvidia stock may struggle to take off if inquiries and government investigations limit its growth appeal, even as demand for its chips remains strong. As a result, I am turning Neutral on Nvidia because I believe its valuation already reflects both its strong chip demand and the regulatory and macro risks ahead.

An SEC Probe Threatens Nvidia's Reporting Structure

I believe investors should brace themselves for increased regulatory scrutiny in the coming months, which is one of the main reasons behind my Neutral stance on the company. There are early warning signs. On November 17, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is conducting a probe into Nvidia to look into its accounting practices and public disclosures to determine whether the chip giant has misled investors. On November 20, The New York Times (NYT) provided more details on this alleged SEC probe.

Specifically, the inquiry is looking into whether Nvidia's 2025 change in how it reports regional results has misled investors. Last year, the company switched from reporting revenue based on customer billing addresses to customer corporate headquarters. This shift entirely removed Singapore as a standalone geographic market for the company.

Given Jensen Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang, who was the controlling shareholder of Singapore-based Megaspeed, the SEC probe is likely to scrutinize this personal relationship. If Nvidia is found to have misled investors, the SEC may penalize the company with fines and even force it to restate its financials. Both outcomes will negatively affect shareholder sentiment.

The Government Probe Is Nowhere Near Complete

In addition to the SEC probe, I believe investors should pay close attention to the ongoing government probe of Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Before CEO Huang's reinstatement, President Trump wrote in a social media post, "Attorney General Todd Blanche has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

detail:
Tech Stock Sell-Off: Down 13%, Is Microsoft a Buy Now?
Patrick Sanders, The Motley Fool

MSFT
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Tech stocks have been hit hard this month as investors worry about the enormous amount of money being spent on artificial intelligence (AI), and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) has been no exception. Shares are down about 13% from their all-time highs.

But I think Microsoft is being unfairly punished here. While many big tech companies are free cash flow negative due to heavy AI spending, Microsoft has affirmed it will remain in the black at least through fiscal 2027.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That's a big deal. And I think it's one reason why the tech sell-off in November presents an attractive buying opportunity for Microsoft before the end of 2026.

Image source: Getty Images.

Microsoft Azure is growing

Microsoft is one of the biggest players in the cloud computing space, holding 21% of the global cloud infrastructure market. That makes Azure the second-largest provider of cloud services behind Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN).

In Microsoft's fiscal first quarter of 2027, which ended Sept. 30, Azure revenue increased 48% from the previous year. Total Microsoft Cloud revenue was $63.9 billion, up 30% from a year ago, and the company's commercial backlog reached $677 billion.

That's an enormous amount of business coming down the line, so Microsoft is spending freely to ensure it has enough computing capacity to meet demand. It spent $45.2 billion on capex in the quarter. But even with that spending, free cash flow remained positive at $18.6 billion. That's because Microsoft generated $58 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, up 29% from a year earlier.

That's a big difference from some other tech companies whose AI spending has pushed free cash flow into negative territory.

Why Microsoft stock looks appealing today

Despite concerns about AI spending, Microsoft's underlying business is performing very well, thanks to its well-known software business. Nearly 4 million companies use Microsoft 365, including its popular office programs such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook.

Those subscriptions provide recurring revenue, while Microsoft's Copilot AI products provide opportunities to sell more services to existing customers. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue increased 17% during the quarter.

That helped Microsoft's fiscal first-quarter revenue increase 19% to $92.3 billion, while operating income climbed 21% to $45.9 billion. Net income was $36.6 billion, up 32% from a year ago.
